Gastroenterology · published research

Atrophic gastritis

One rat experiment, reported in two papers, found better mucosal structure and acid secretion at the lowest tested fluence. Higher fluences did not show the same pattern, and clinical evidence is absent.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One rat experiment, reported in two papers, found better mucosal structure and acid secretion at the lowest tested fluence. Higher fluences did not show the same pattern, and clinical evidence is absent.

Summary of the Evidence

Two 2005 publications describe He-Ne laser treatment for chronic atrophic gastritis in rats. Their authors, disease-induction method, three fluence groups, and 20-day schedule closely match, and one report adds cyclin-D1 measurements. They appear to be companion reports from one 63-rat experiment, not two independent studies. No human trial, animal replication, or separate cell study was identified in this exact category.

Human and clinical evidence

No human PBM study for atrophic gastritis was identified. The measured outcomes—gastric acid secretion, mucosal thickness, inflammatory cells, and parietal-cell morphology—are experimental tissue or physiological measures, not patient symptoms, endoscopic progression, or cancer risk.

Animal evidence

In the Wistar-rat model, 633-nm helium-neon light was applied over the stomach projection. At 3.36 J/cm² daily for 20 days, gastric acid secretion increased, the gastric mucosa became thicker, inflammatory-cell infiltration decreased, and parietal-cell structure moved toward normal compared with untreated model controls. The Chinese-language companion report also found higher cyclin-D1 expression at this fluence. The 4.80- and 6.24-J/cm² groups did not show comparable improvement, so the result was not a simple “more light, more effect” pattern (Shao et al. 2005; Yang et al. 2005).

The result is compatible with a fluence-specific response in this model, but it is based on one experiment and has not been independently reproduced. Cyclin-D1 and tissue appearance alone do not establish lasting recovery of the gastric glands or reduced disease progression.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct cell-culture or ex-vivo study of PBM for atrophic gastritis was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The two papers report a 633-nm He-Ne laser, in the red visible range, with three fluences of 3.36, 4.80, and 6.24 J/cm² given once daily for 20 days. The lowest tested fluence was the one associated with improved reported outcomes. The papers do not establish a human delivery method, and no dose-finding study has confirmed an optimal range.

Interpretation

The reported changes at 3.36 J/cm² are favorable within a chemically induced rat model, while higher tested fluences did not reproduce the same pattern. Because both publications appear to describe the same experiment, the evidence should be counted as one study. It cannot yet show whether PBM changes the course or clinical consequences of atrophic gastritis in people.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for gastric mucosal and acid-secretion outcomes in rats
Publications and records2 articles (one rat experiment reported twice)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A low-dose He-Ne protocol improved gastric thickness, inflammatory-cell counts, parietal-cell appearance, and acid secretion in one rat experiment. Two papers appear to report that same experiment, rather than two replications. The result has not been confirmed in another laboratory or in people. Independent replication with disease-relevant and longer-term outcomes is needed to support a stronger conclusion.
